title: Hypergeometric Probabilities
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter covers the derivation and application of the hypergeometric distribution through classical counting arguments. It assumes familiarity with basic combinatorics, particularly binomial coefficients and the discrete uniform probability law over finite sample spaces. ## The Sampling Model Consider an urn containing $n$ total items (represented as balls). The items are partitioned into two distinct categories: - $m$ "red" items of interest, and - $n - m$ "black" (or non-red) items. Suppose we draw a sample of $k$ items at random without replacement from the urn. We want to determine the probability $p_r$ that our sample contains exactly $i$ red items (and therefore $k - i$ black items). ## Derivation via Counting Because every subset of $k$ items drawn from the pool of $n$ items is equally likely, we apply the discrete uniform probability law: $$p_r = \frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}} = \frac{c}{|\Omega|}$$ ### 1. Size of the Sample Space The sample space $\Omega$ consists of all possible unordered subsets of size $k$ chosen from a collection of $n$ items. The total number of outcomes is: $$|\Omega| = \binom{n}{k}$$ ### 2. Size of the Event of Interest Let $c$ denote the number of outcomes containing exactly $i$ red items and $k - i$ black items. We construct such a sample in two independent selection steps: 1. **Select the red items:** Choose $i$ red items from the available $m$ red items. The number of ways to do this is: $$a = \binom{m}{i}$$ 2. **Select the black items:** Choose the remaining $k - i$ items from the available $n - m$ black items. The number of ways to do this is: $$b = \binom{n - m}{k - i}$$ By the counting principle, the total number of favorable outcomes $c$ is the product $a \times b$: $$c = \binom{m}{i} \binom{n - m}{k - i}$$ ### 3. Hypergeometric Probability Formula Dividing the number of favorable outcomes $c$ by the total size of the sample space $|\Omega|$ gives the hypergeometric probability: $$p_r = \frac{\binom{m}{i} \binom{n - m}{k - i}}{\binom{n}{k}}$$ ## Example: Dealing Aces from a Standard Deck Consider drawing cards from a standard deck: - Total number of cards: $n = 52$ - Number of aces in the deck: $m = 4$ - Number of non-aces: $n - m = 48$ Suppose we draw a hand of $k = 7$ cards without replacement. We wish to find the probability of obtaining exactly $i = 3$ aces (and thus $k - i = 7 - 3 = 4$ non-aces). Casting this directly into the hypergeometric framework: - Number of ways to choose $3$ aces from $4$: $\binom{4}{3}$ - Number of ways to choose $4$ non-aces from $48$: $\binom{48}{4}$ - Total number of ways to draw $7$ cards from $52$: $\binom{52}{7}$ The probability is: $$p_r = \frac{\binom{4}{3} \binom{48}{4}}{\binom{52}{7}}$$ ## Sources - Recitation transcript "Hypergeometric Probabilities" (6.041SC Fall 2013): formulation of the urn model, derivation of the counting formula $a \times b / |\Omega|$, and the 52-card deck worked example.
